title: Narrowing down a bug
summary: When there is no error to read, reproduce the bug, cut the system in half, and let git bisect find the commit that broke it.
youWillLearn: How to turn "it's broken sometimes" into steps that fail every time
How to isolate a bug by testing one half of the system at a time
Binary search with log probes inside your own code
How git bisect finds the exact commit that broke something

glossary.reproduce: To find exact steps that make the bug happen every time you follow them.
glossary.isolate: To test one part of the system on its own, so a result can only be explained by that part.
glossary.binary search: Finding something by checking the middle, keeping the half that contains it, and repeating. Each check halves what is left.
glossary.probe: A temporary log line placed at one point in the code to check whether the data is still correct there.
glossary.commit: A saved snapshot of the code in git, with an id like 9f2e1aa and a message describing the change.
glossary.git bisect: A git command that runs a binary search through your commit history to find the first commit where a bug appears.
glossary.regression: A bug in something that used to work, introduced by a later change.

steps.title: Blank summaries, and no error anywhere
body: Since sometime this week, Notely's AI summaries come back blank. No red in the Console. Network shows a 200. The Vercel logs show no errors.
Nothing to read, so the last three lessons do not point anywhere. The bug could be in the page, the route, the database or the Claude call. You need a method, not a guess.

scene.caption: No errors anywhere. Every part of the system is a suspect.

steps.title: Shrink the haystack, half at a time
body: Do not search for the bug. Search for where it is not. Pick a test whose answer rules out a big part of the system, ideally half.
Each test cuts the suspects down. A handful of good tests corners almost any bug, even in a codebase you did not write yourself, which with Claude Code is often the case.

callout.text: A string of fairy lights goes dark. You do not test every bulb. You check the middle of the string: power there? Then the fault is in the second half. Check its middle. Repeat.

scene.caption: One test at the right point clears half the suspects at once.

steps.title: Step one: make it fail on demand
body: A bug you cannot reproduce is a bug you cannot prove fixed. Write down the exact steps, and vary one thing at a time: another note, another user, another browser, local instead of production.
Maya finds it fails for every note, for every user, locally too. Good news: not about data, not about Vercel settings, and she can test on her laptop.

code.code:
1. Log in as maya@example.com (local or prod)
2. Open any note, e.g. n_81
3. Click "AI summary"
Expected: 3-line summary
Actual:   empty box, status 200, no error
Since:    worked last Monday

scene.caption: Reliable repro: every note, every user, locally too. Data and hosting settings are ruled out.

steps.title: Isolate: skip the page entirely
body: Now isolate: test half A without half B. Call the route directly from the terminal, with no page involved. If the raw answer is already wrong, the page is innocent.
It is: the route returns {}, with no summary field at all. The page was faithfully showing nothing. The bug lives on the server side.

code.caption: If the route needs a login, add your local cookie from DevTools with -H "Cookie: …". Never share that command.

scene.caption: Called directly, the route already returns an empty object. The page is cleared.

steps.title: Binary search inside the route
body: The route has three stages: load the note, call Claude, build the reply. Put a probe in the middle: log the raw Claude response, then run the same curl.
The response has content[0].text with a full summary. So loading and calling work. The bug is in the last stage. That is binary search: test the middle, keep the bad half.

code.caption: Mark probes with PROBE so they are easy to find. This one prints note content: run it locally only and delete it before committing.

scene.caption: A probe after the Claude call shows good data, so the bug is in building the reply.

steps.title: git bisect: binary search through time
body: It worked last Monday, so this is a regression: some commit since then broke it. Git bisect finds which one.
You name one good commit and one bad one. Git checks out the commit halfway between. You test it and say good or bad. Git halves again. Even 100 commits take only about 7 tests.

code.code:
git bisect start
git bisect bad              # the current commit is broken
git bisect good a1b2c3d     # last Monday's commit worked
# git checks out a commit in the middle. Test it, then:
git bisect good             # or: git bisect bad
# ...repeat until git prints "is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset            # back to where you started
code.caption: If a script can tell good from bad, git bisect run <script> does the testing for you.

scene.caption: The commits since Monday. Git checks out the one in the middle for you to test.

steps.title: The first bad commit, found
body: c48f019 works: mark it good. Git jumps to 9f2e1aa. Blank summary: mark it bad. Git prints: 9f2e1aa is the first bad commit, "refactor summary types".
The diff is one line. The refactor read .value, a field that does not exist. undefined silently drops out of JSON, so the route sent {}.

callout.text: Vercel keeps every deployment at its own URL. Opening an older deployment is a quick way to confirm which commit was still good before you start bisecting.

code.caption: SummaryBlock said value, but the API sends text. res.json() gives untyped data, so TypeScript trusts whatever shape the as cast claims.

scene.caption: Two tests later, git names the first bad commit: 9f2e1aa.

steps.title: Change one thing, then test
body: Narrowing only works if each test changes one thing. Edit three files, restart, and it works? You no longer know which edit fixed it, or whether one of them broke something else.
Same while bisecting: no fixes until git has named the commit. Then run git bisect reset, make the fix on your normal branch, and re-run the repro steps from the start.

callout.text: Claude Code likes to change several files at once. Ask it to reproduce first, then propose one change and say what result would prove it right. Check git diff --stat: a one-line bug should get a small diff. And ask it to remove every PROBE line before committing.

scene.caption: One small fix on top of today's code, tested with the same repro steps.

steps.title: Recap: a method beats a hunch
body: Reproduce until it fails every time. Isolate by testing one half of the system, like calling the route without the page. Binary search inside the code with probes.
When it used to work, let git bisect find the first bad commit. Change one thing per test, and prove the fix with the same repro steps.

quiz.question: A client says bookings "sometimes" fail. You cannot make it happen. What is the best first move?

options.text: Ask Claude Code to add retries to every database call.
options.why: That guesses at a cause you have not found, and may hide the real one.

options.text: Collect exact cases: which user, which time slot, which device, and what they saw.
options.why: "Sometimes" usually means "under conditions we have not noticed yet". Finding them is how you get a reliable repro.

options.text: Rewrite the booking flow, since it is clearly fragile.
options.why: A rewrite without knowing the cause can carry the same bug over, and you cannot prove it is gone.

quiz.question: The page shows a wrong price. You call the API route with curl and the price in the response is correct. What have you learned?

options.text: The bug is on the server side, in how the price is calculated.
options.why: The server sent the right price, so its calculation is fine.

options.text: Nothing, since curl and the browser behave differently.
options.why: The route's answer does not depend on who asks, unless login or headers differ. A matching request is a fair test.

options.text: The bug is in the page: how it reads or displays the price.
options.why: The server half is cleared. Whatever goes wrong happens after the response arrives in the browser.

quiz.question: A feature worked 120 commits ago and is broken now. Roughly how many tests does git bisect need to find the first bad commit?

options.why: Each test halves the range: 120, 60, 30, 15, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is about 7 tests.
That would be a straight walk through history. Bisect jumps to the middle each time instead.
Testing every commit is exactly the slow path bisect saves you from.

takeaways: First reproduce: exact steps that fail every time. Without them you cannot prove a fix.
Isolate by testing one half of the system, for example curl the route to skip the page.
Inside the code, place a PROBE log in the middle and keep the half where the data goes wrong.
When it used to work, git bisect finds the first bad commit in a handful of tests.
Change one thing per test, and remove probes before you commit.
